# How to use this guide

Human Anatomy and Physiology I is a "draw and explain" subject. Examiners give a large share of the marks for a neat labelled diagram, a clear sequence of steps (for example, the clotting cascade or the steps of muscle contraction) and correct normal values. Study one unit at a time: read the notes, redraw every text diagram from memory on rough paper, learn the tables of normal values, then answer the question bank before checking the model answers. Finish each unit with its MCQs.

The five units follow the five units of the PCI syllabus exactly; no unit has been split or joined. Unit 2 is the longest because it holds three syllabus topics (skin, skeleton with skeletal muscle, and joints). The 15 practical guides cover the BP107P practical list.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ or very short answers | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

The question bank has long essays (10 marks), short answers (5 marks) and very short answers (2 marks, useful for class tests and sessionals).

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with a diagram and normal values.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Body, cells, tissues | Structure of cell with organelles, transport across the membrane, homeostasis with feedback, classification of epithelial and connective tissue, cell junctions, forms of cell signalling |
| 2 Skin, skeleton, joints | Structure and functions of skin, classification of bones, skull and vertebral column, sliding filament theory, neuromuscular junction, classification of joints with synovial joint diagram |
| 3 Blood and lymph | Composition and functions of blood, haemopoiesis, haemoglobin, coagulation cascade, blood groups and Rh factor, anaemia, lymph node and lymphatic system |
| 4 PNS and special senses | Sympathetic vs parasympathetic, cranial nerves table, spinal nerves and plexuses, structure of eye and ear with mechanism of vision and hearing, disorders |
| 5 Cardiovascular system | Structure of heart, conduction system, cardiac cycle, cardiac output, regulation of BP, ECG, artery vs vein |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Put a diagram in every long answer, even if the question does not ask for one: cell, epithelium, long bone, sarcomere, NMJ, synovial joint, blood cells, lymph node, ANS outflow, eye, ear, heart, conduction system, ECG. Label at least six parts; neat labels with straight lines score more than artistic shading.
2. Begin with a one-line definition, then a table or flow chart. Flow charts suit sequences: haemopoiesis, clotting cascade, muscle contraction, baroreceptor reflex, RAAS, hearing.
3. Quote standard normal values: RBC 4.5–5.5 million/mm³, WBC 4,000–11,000/mm³, platelets 1.5–4 lakh/mm³, Hb 14–18 g/dL (men), BP 120/80 mmHg, heart rate 72/min, cardiac output 5 L/min, cardiac cycle 0.8 s, PR interval 0.12–0.20 s.
4. Use comparison tables for "differentiate" questions: sympathetic vs parasympathetic, artery vs vein, skeletal vs cardiac vs smooth muscle, mitosis vs meiosis, intrinsic vs extrinsic pathway.
5. End with two or three applied points — a disorder or a drug that acts at that site (neostigmine at the NMJ, warfarin and vitamin K factors, ACE inhibitors and RAAS, atropine and heart rate). Pharmacy examiners look for this link.
6. Learn the counts that MCQs love: 206 bones, 22 skull bones, 33 vertebrae in a child and 26 in an adult, 31 pairs of spinal nerves, 12 pairs of cranial nerves, 13 clotting factors with no VI, 3 ear ossicles.
7. For the cranial nerves, practise writing the full table (number, name, type, origin, function) in under ten minutes.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, learn these five answers with full diagrams: **structure of cell and transport across the membrane**, **sliding filament theory with the neuromuscular junction**, **mechanism of coagulation**, **sympathetic vs parasympathetic nervous system**, and **conduction system with the cardiac cycle**. Then revise the tables below.

**Diagrams to draw once tonight**

| Unit | Diagram |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Cell with organelles; simple and stratified epithelium; neuron |
| 2 | Layers of skin; long bone; sarcomere; NMJ; synovial joint |
| 3 | Blood cells; coagulation cascade; lymph node |
| 4 | ANS outflow; eyeball (sagittal section); ear |
| 5 | Heart with chambers and valves; conduction system; normal ECG |

**Numbers worth memorising**

| Fact | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Total body water | About 60% of body weight (ICF 2/3, ECF 1/3) |
| Blood volume | 5–6 L; pH 7.35–7.45 |
| Plasma : cells | 55 : 45 |
| RBC count | 4.5–5.5 million/mm³ (men), 4.0–5.0 million/mm³ (women); life 120 days |
| WBC count | 4,000–11,000/mm³ |
| Differential count | N 50–70%, L 20–40%, M 2–8%, E 1–4%, B 0–1% |
| Platelets | 1.5–4 lakh/mm³; life about 7–10 days |
| Haemoglobin | 14–18 g/dL (men), 12–16 g/dL (women) |
| Bleeding time / clotting time | 1–5 min / about 3–8 min (capillary tube) |
| Bones | 206 (axial 80, appendicular 126); skull 22 |
| Vertebrae | 7 C, 12 T, 5 L, sacrum (5 fused), coccyx (4 fused) |
| Ribs | True 1–7, false 8–10, floating 11–12 |
| Spinal nerves | 31 pairs (8 C, 12 T, 5 L, 5 S, 1 Co) |
| Cranial nerves | 12 pairs |
| Heart rate | 72/min (60–100) |
| Cardiac output | About 5 L/min (SV 70 ml × HR 72) |
| Cardiac cycle | 0.8 s (ventricular systole 0.3, diastole 0.5) |
| Blood pressure | 120/80 mmHg; pulse pressure 40; MAP about 93 |
| ECG | PR 0.12–0.20 s; QRS under 0.12 s; QT about 0.36–0.44 s |
| Na+/K+ pump | 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP |

**One-line facts**

1. Negative feedback restores normal (BP, temperature); positive feedback amplifies (labour, clotting).
2. Forms of signalling: contact-dependent, paracrine, synaptic, endocrine; second messengers cAMP, IP3/DAG, Ca2+.
3. Epithelium is avascular and sits on a basement membrane; transitional epithelium lines the bladder.
4. Epidermis from deep: basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum, corneum; skin makes vitamin D3.
5. Atlas (C1) holds the skull; axis (C2) has the dens; patella is the largest sesamoid bone; femur is the longest bone.
6. Sarcomere = Z to Z; Ca2+ binds troponin C; ATP detaches myosin; acetylcholine acts on nicotinic receptors at the NMJ.
7. Synovial joints: plane, hinge, pivot, condyloid, saddle (thumb), ball and socket (shoulder, hip).
8. Erythropoietin comes from the kidney; vitamin B12, folic acid and iron are needed; reticulocyte precedes the mature RBC.
9. Hb = 4 globin chains + 4 haems; breakdown → bilirubin.
10. Clotting factors II, VII, IX, X need vitamin K; factor IV = Ca2+; no factor VI; haemophilia A = factor VIII.
11. O is the universal donor, AB the universal recipient; anti-D immunoglobulin within 72 hours of delivery.
12. Thoracic duct drains into the left subclavian vein; Kupffer cells, microglia and alveolar macrophages belong to the RES.
13. Sympathetic: T1–L2, short pre / long post, noradrenaline. Parasympathetic: III, VII, IX, X and S2–S4, acetylcholine.
14. Phrenic C3–C5; sciatic is the largest nerve; I, II, VIII purely sensory cranial nerves.
15. Rods need vitamin A; myopia → concave lens; glaucoma = raised intraocular pressure; organ of Corti = hearing.
16. SA node → AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres; AV delay about 0.1 s.
17. S1 = closure of AV valves; S2 = closure of semilunar valves.
18. BP = CO × peripheral resistance; baroreceptors in carotid sinus and aortic arch; angiotensin II constricts vessels and releases aldosterone.

# Study of the compound microscope

**Aim:** To study the parts, working and care of a compound microscope and to focus a slide under low power, high power and oil immersion.

> Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Carry the microscope with both hands.

## Principle

A compound microscope uses two lens systems. The **objective** forms a real, inverted, magnified image of the object; the **eyepiece (ocular)** magnifies this image further to give a virtual, inverted, enlarged final image.

**Total magnification = magnification of objective × magnification of eyepiece.**

**Resolving power** is the ability to show two close points as separate. It improves with a higher numerical aperture (NA) of the objective and with shorter wavelength of light. Under the oil-immersion lens, a drop of immersion oil (cedarwood oil or synthetic oil with a refractive index close to glass, about 1.5) prevents light from bending away in air, so more light enters the objective and resolution improves.

## Requirements

Compound microscope, prepared permanent slides (e.g. stained blood smear), immersion oil, lens paper, xylene (for cleaning oil, used sparingly).

## Parts of the microscope

```text
              EYEPIECE (10x)
                 |
              Body tube
                 |
   Arm ---    Revolving nosepiece
   (limb)     /   |    \
          10x   40x   100x (oil)  OBJECTIVES
                 |
           ===== STAGE ===== (stage clips / mechanical stage)
              Condenser + iris diaphragm
                 |
           Mirror / built-in lamp
   Coarse adjustment knob, fine adjustment knob on the side
              BASE (foot)
```

| Part | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Base and arm | Support; arm is used to carry the instrument |
| Body tube | Holds eyepiece and objectives at the correct distance |
| Eyepiece | Magnifies the image from the objective (usually 10×) |
| Revolving nosepiece | Carries objectives; rotates to change them |
| Objectives | Low power 10×, high power 40×, oil immersion 100× (some also 4× scanning) |
| Stage and clips / mechanical stage | Hold and move the slide |
| Condenser | Focuses light on the object |
| Iris diaphragm | Controls the amount of light |
| Mirror or lamp | Light source (plane mirror with daylight, concave without condenser) |
| Coarse adjustment | Large up-down movement for rough focusing |
| Fine adjustment | Small movement for sharp focus |

## Procedure

1. Place the microscope on a firm table with the arm towards you. Clean lenses with lens paper only.
2. Turn the low-power (10×) objective into line. Adjust the mirror or lamp, open the iris diaphragm and raise the condenser until the field is evenly bright.
3. Place the slide on the stage, cover-slip up, and fix it with clips so the specimen is over the hole.
4. Watching from the side, lower the objective with the coarse knob until it is close to the slide.
5. Looking through the eyepiece, raise the objective slowly with the coarse knob until the specimen appears; sharpen with the fine knob.
6. Bring the area of interest to the centre. Rotate to high power (40×) and focus with the **fine knob only**; adjust light.
7. For oil immersion: raise the objective slightly, put one drop of oil on the slide, turn the 100× objective into place so it dips into the oil, and focus with the fine knob. Use full light (condenser up, diaphragm open).
8. After use, wipe oil off the objective and slide with lens paper (a trace of xylene if needed), lower the stage, return to low power and cover the microscope.

## Observations

| Objective | Eyepiece | Total magnification | Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10× | 10× | 100× | Locating the specimen, tissue layers |
| 40× | 10× | 400× | Cell details, counting chambers |
| 100× (oil) | 10× | 1000× | Blood cells, bacteria |

## Result

The parts and working of the compound microscope were studied, and the slide was focused under low power (100×), high power (400×) and oil immersion (1000×).

## Precautions

1. Never focus downwards with the coarse knob while looking through the eyepiece; the objective may break the slide.
2. Use only the fine knob under high power and oil immersion.
3. Do not touch lenses with fingers; clean with lens paper.
4. Remove oil from the oil-immersion lens immediately after use.
5. Carry the microscope upright with one hand on the arm and one under the base.

## Viva questions

1. **How is total magnification calculated?** Objective magnification × eyepiece magnification.
2. **Why is oil used with the 100× objective?** Oil has a refractive index close to glass, so light is not lost by refraction and resolution improves.
3. **What is resolving power?** The ability to distinguish two close points as separate; it depends on numerical aperture and wavelength.
4. **What is the function of the condenser?** It concentrates light onto the specimen.
5. **What kind of image does a compound microscope form?** A magnified, virtual, inverted final image.
6. **Which knob is used under high power?** The fine adjustment knob only.

# Microscopic study of epithelial and connective tissue

**Aim:** To identify and draw permanent slides of epithelial and connective tissues and to note their identifying features.

> Slides available differ between colleges. Draw what you see under low and high power, and label it.

## Principle

Tissues are identified by the shape and arrangement of cells, the number of layers, the amount of matrix and special features (cilia, goblet cells, fibres, lacunae). Haematoxylin stains nuclei blue-purple; eosin stains cytoplasm and fibres pink.

## Requirements

Compound microscope; permanent stained slides (simple squamous, simple cuboidal, simple columnar, ciliated pseudostratified columnar, stratified squamous, transitional epithelium; areolar tissue, adipose tissue, dense regular tissue such as tendon, hyaline cartilage, compact bone T.S.); drawing sheets and pencil.

## Procedure

1. Focus each slide under low power (10×) to see the general arrangement.
2. Move to high power (40×) to see cell shape, nuclei and special features.
3. Draw a labelled diagram of a representative area and write the identifying points.

## Observations: identifying features

| Slide | Identifying features | Location in body |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Simple squamous epithelium | Single layer of thin flat cells with flattened central nuclei; looks like floor tiles in surface view | Alveoli, blood vessel lining, Bowman's capsule |
| Simple cuboidal epithelium | Single layer of square cells with round central nuclei, often around a lumen | Kidney tubules, thyroid follicles |
| Simple columnar epithelium | Single layer of tall cells with oval nuclei near the base; goblet cells; may have a brush border | Stomach, intestine |
| Pseudostratified ciliated columnar | Nuclei at different levels so it looks layered, but all cells touch the basement membrane; cilia and goblet cells | Trachea, bronchi |
| Stratified squamous epithelium | Many layers; basal cells cuboidal or columnar, surface cells flat; keratin layer on skin | Skin, oesophagus, mouth |
| Transitional epithelium | Several layers; large rounded "dome" or umbrella cells at the surface | Urinary bladder, ureter |
| Areolar tissue | Loose network of thin pink collagen and fine dark elastic fibres; scattered fibroblasts, mast cells, macrophages | Under the skin, around organs |
| Adipose tissue | Large empty-looking cells (fat dissolved in processing) with the nucleus pressed to one side ("signet ring") | Subcutaneous tissue |
| Dense regular (tendon) | Parallel wavy collagen bundles with rows of flattened fibroblast nuclei | Tendons, ligaments |
| Hyaline cartilage | Glassy homogeneous matrix; chondrocytes in lacunae, often in groups of two or four; perichondrium | Trachea, articular surfaces |
| Compact bone (T.S.) | Osteons: central Haversian canal surrounded by concentric lamellae; lacunae with canaliculi like a spider pattern | Shaft of long bones |

```text
Simple columnar        Stratified squamous       Hyaline cartilage     Compact bone (osteon)
|o||o||o||o|            ~~~~~~~~~~ (flat)        .  (oo)    .            @@@@@
|  ||  ||  |            oooooooooo               (oo)   (o)             @ (O) @   O = Haversian canal
==basement==            [o][o][o] (basal)         glassy matrix          @@@@@     rings = lamellae
```

## Result

The given slides of epithelial and connective tissue were observed and identified by their characteristic features, and labelled diagrams were drawn.

## Precautions

1. Always locate the tissue under low power before switching to high power.
2. Handle slides by the edges; clean them before returning.
3. Draw only what is seen, with a pencil, and label on one side.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the basement membrane?** A thin non-cellular layer on which epithelium rests, joining it to connective tissue.
2. **Why is epithelium called avascular?** It has no blood vessels; it is nourished by diffusion from underlying connective tissue.
3. **What is pseudostratified epithelium?** A single layer that looks stratified because nuclei lie at different heights.
4. **Which cells make fibres in connective tissue?** Fibroblasts.
5. **What are lacunae?** Small spaces in the matrix of cartilage or bone that contain chondrocytes or osteocytes.
6. **Why do fat cells look empty in a slide?** The fat dissolves in the alcohol and xylene used to prepare the slide.

# Microscopic study of muscular and nervous tissue

**Aim:** To identify and draw permanent slides of skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle and of nervous tissue.

> Use the slides provided in your laboratory; labels and staining may vary.

## Principle

Muscle types differ in fibre shape, number and position of nuclei, striations and special junctions. Nervous tissue is recognised by neurons with cell bodies and processes, and by myelinated fibres or nerve bundles.

## Requirements

Compound microscope; permanent slides of skeletal muscle (L.S. and T.S.), cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, multipolar neurons (spinal cord smear or section), peripheral nerve (T.S.); drawing sheets.

## Procedure

1. Scan each slide under low power, then study details under high power.
2. Note shape of fibres, nuclei, striations, branching and special structures.
3. Draw and label a representative field.

## Observations

| Slide | Identifying features |
| --- | --- |
| Skeletal muscle (L.S.) | Long unbranched cylindrical fibres; many oval nuclei at the periphery under the sarcolemma; clear alternate dark (A) and light (I) cross-striations |
| Skeletal muscle (T.S.) | Polygonal fibre profiles grouped into fascicles by perimysium; peripheral nuclei |
| Cardiac muscle | Branched fibres joined end to end; one or two central nuclei; faint striations; dark transverse **intercalated discs** |
| Smooth muscle | Spindle-shaped fibres with tapering ends; single central rod-shaped nucleus; no striations; packed in sheets |
| Multipolar neuron | Large cell body with a prominent nucleus and nucleolus; Nissl granules in cytoplasm; several dendrites and one axon |
| Peripheral nerve (T.S.) | Bundles (fascicles) of nerve fibres surrounded by perineurium, whole nerve by epineurium; each fibre with a central axon and pale myelin ring |

```text
Skeletal (L.S.)          Cardiac                    Smooth           Multipolar neuron
|||||||||||||  o         ===o===||==o=====          <==o==>            \ | /
|||||||||||||  o  (edge     \        /  (|| =         <==o==>          (  O  )--axon-->
|||||||||||||     nuclei)    ==o==||=== intercalated  <==o==>            / | \
 striations                 branched     disc)      spindle cells     dendrites
```

**Comparison**

| Feature | Skeletal | Cardiac | Smooth |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Shape | Cylindrical | Branched | Spindle |
| Nuclei | Many, peripheral | One or two, central | One, central |
| Striations | Present | Present | Absent |
| Intercalated discs | Absent | Present | Absent |
| Control | Voluntary | Involuntary | Involuntary |

## Result

Skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle and nervous tissue were observed and identified by their characteristic features, and labelled diagrams were drawn.

## Precautions

1. Focus under low power first.
2. Adjust the light to see striations clearly (reduce light with the diaphragm).
3. Draw neatly with labels.

## Viva questions

1. **What are intercalated discs?** Specialised junctions (desmosomes and gap junctions) joining cardiac muscle cells, allowing the heart to contract as one unit.
2. **Why is skeletal muscle striated?** Regular arrangement of actin and myosin filaments in sarcomeres produces light and dark bands.
3. **What are Nissl granules?** Clumps of rough ER and ribosomes in the neuron cell body, sites of protein synthesis.
4. **What forms myelin in peripheral nerves?** Schwann cells.
5. **Which muscle has a single central nucleus and no striations?** Smooth muscle.

# Identification of axial bones

**Aim:** To identify the bones of the axial skeleton (skull, vertebrae, ribs, sternum, hyoid) and to describe their important features.

> Use the dry bones or models in your laboratory. Handle skulls gently; thin bones such as the ethmoid break easily.

## Principle

The axial skeleton (80 bones) forms the central axis of the body: skull 22, hyoid 1, ear ossicles 6, vertebral column 26 and thoracic cage 25 (sternum 1 + ribs 24). Each bone is identified by its shape, size and landmarks (processes, foramina, facets).

## Requirements

Articulated skull and disarticulated skull bones (or models), typical and special vertebrae, sacrum, coccyx, sternum, typical and atypical ribs, hyoid bone; record book.

## Procedure

1. Examine each specimen; note its general shape and size.
2. Identify the region from its features (use the tables below).
3. Locate and name the important landmarks.
4. Draw a labelled outline of each bone and write its identifying points and functions.

## Observations

**Skull**

| Bone | Identifying features |
| --- | --- |
| Frontal | Forehead; supraorbital margins; frontal sinuses inside |
| Parietal (2) | Square, curved plates forming roof and sides; meet at the sagittal suture |
| Temporal (2) | External acoustic meatus; mastoid process behind it; styloid process; zygomatic process; houses middle and inner ear |
| Occipital | Back and base; foramen magnum; occipital condyles articulate with the atlas |
| Sphenoid | Bat or butterfly shape across the base; sella turcica holding the pituitary |
| Ethmoid | Light, between the orbits; cribriform plate with many small holes for olfactory nerves; crista galli |
| Maxilla (2) | Upper jaw with upper teeth; part of hard palate; large maxillary sinus |
| Mandible | U-shaped lower jaw; body, ramus, condylar and coronoid processes, mental foramen; only movable skull bone |
| Zygomatic, nasal, lacrimal, palatine, vomer, inferior conchae | Cheek, bridge of nose, medial orbit wall, back of hard palate, lower nasal septum, side walls of nose |

**Vertebrae**

| Specimen | Identifying features |
| --- | --- |
| Typical cervical | Small oval body, large triangular vertebral foramen, **foramen transversarium** in each transverse process, bifid spine |
| Atlas (C1) | Ring-like; no body and no spine; large superior facets for occipital condyles |
| Axis (C2) | **Dens** (odontoid process) projecting upward from the body |
| C7 (vertebra prominens) | Long, non-bifid spine felt at the base of the neck |
| Thoracic | Heart-shaped body; **costal facets** on body and transverse processes for ribs; long spine pointing downward; round foramen |
| Lumbar | Large kidney-shaped body; short, thick, horizontal spine; no costal facets or transverse foramina |
| Sacrum | Triangular, five fused vertebrae; four pairs of sacral foramina; sacral promontory; ear-shaped auricular surface for the hip bone |
| Coccyx | Small triangular bone of usually four fused pieces |

**Thoracic cage and hyoid**

| Specimen | Identifying features |
| --- | --- |
| Sternum | Flat dagger-shaped bone: manubrium (jugular notch, clavicular notches), body (notches for costal cartilages), xiphoid process |
| Typical rib (3rd to 9th) | Curved flat bone with head (two facets), neck, tubercle, angle and shaft; costal groove on the inner lower border for intercostal vessels and nerve |
| First rib | Shortest, broadest, most curved; flat surfaces face up and down; groove for subclavian vessels |
| Floating ribs (11, 12) | Short; no tubercle; free anterior end |
| Hyoid | U-shaped; body with greater and lesser horns; does not articulate with other bones |

## Result

The bones of the axial skeleton were identified and their important features recorded.

## Precautions

1. Handle bones with both hands over the table; never hold a skull by the eye sockets.
2. Do not mark bones with pen or pencil.
3. Return bones to the correct box.

## Viva questions

1. **How many bones form the axial skeleton?** 80.
2. **Which bone has the sella turcica?** Sphenoid; it lodges the pituitary gland.
3. **What passes through the foramen magnum?** The spinal cord (lower end of medulla) with its coverings and vertebral arteries.
4. **How is a cervical vertebra identified?** By the foramen transversarium in its transverse process.
5. **Which vertebra has no body?** Atlas (C1).
6. **Which ribs are called floating ribs?** The 11th and 12th, which have no anterior attachment.
7. **Which bone does not articulate with any other bone?** Hyoid.

# Identification of appendicular bones

**Aim:** To identify the bones of the upper and lower limbs and their girdles, and to determine the side (right or left) of long bones.

> Use the dry bones or models in your laboratory. Ask your teacher to confirm side determination the first time.

## Principle

The appendicular skeleton (126 bones) has the pectoral girdles and upper limbs (64) and the pelvic girdle and lower limbs (62). Long bones have a proximal end, a shaft and a distal end; the landmarks on the ends tell the bone and its side.

**Side determination:** hold the bone as it lies in your own body — upper end up, front facing forward (away from you), back facing you. The structures that lie laterally (such as the greater tubercle of the humerus, greater trochanter of the femur) are then on the bone's true lateral side. If the lateral feature is on your right, it is a right bone.

## Requirements

Clavicle, scapula, humerus, radius, ulna, articulated hand, hip bone, femur, patella, tibia, fibula, articulated foot (or models); record book.

## Procedure

1. Identify each bone from its general shape.
2. Locate proximal and distal ends, anterior and posterior surfaces, medial and lateral sides.
3. Name the important landmarks and determine the side of long bones.
4. Draw a labelled outline and write the identifying points.

## Observations

**Upper limb**

| Bone | Identifying features | Side clue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clavicle | S-shaped; medial end rounded (sternal), lateral end flat (acromial) | Medial two-thirds convex forward; inferior surface rough |
| Scapula | Triangular flat bone; spine on the back ending in the acromion; coracoid process; glenoid cavity at the lateral angle | Glenoid cavity is lateral; spine is on the posterior surface |
| Humerus | Rounded head, anatomical and surgical necks, greater and lesser tubercles with intertubercular groove, deltoid tuberosity; distal capitulum, trochlea, olecranon fossa behind | Head faces medially; greater tubercle lateral; olecranon fossa posterior |
| Ulna | Upper end like a hook: olecranon and coronoid processes with the trochlear notch; small distal head with styloid process | Trochlear notch faces forward; radial notch is lateral |
| Radius | Small disc-shaped upper head; radial tuberosity; wide distal end with styloid process laterally | Styloid process lateral (thumb side) |
| Carpals (8) | Two rows: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate (hook) | — |
| Metacarpals (5), phalanges (14) | Palm bones; thumb has two phalanges, fingers three | — |

**Lower limb**

| Bone | Identifying features | Side clue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hip bone | Large irregular bone of ilium, ischium and pubis fused at the cup-shaped **acetabulum**; obturator foramen below; iliac crest above | Acetabulum faces laterally; obturator foramen lies below and in front of it |
| Femur | Longest bone; rounded head on an angled neck, greater and lesser trochanters, linea aspera behind the shaft; medial and lateral condyles | Head medial; greater trochanter lateral; linea aspera posterior |
| Patella | Triangular sesamoid bone with apex down; lateral articular facet larger | Larger lateral facet |
| Tibia | Large medial leg bone; flat upper condyles, tibial tuberosity in front, sharp anterior border (shin), **medial malleolus** at the lower end | Medial malleolus medial; tuberosity anterior |
| Fibula | Thin lateral bone; head at the top; **lateral malleolus** at the lower end with a pit (malleolar fossa) behind | Malleolar fossa posterior and medial |
| Tarsals (7) | Talus, calcaneus (heel, largest), navicular, cuboid, three cuneiforms | — |
| Metatarsals (5), phalanges (14) | Foot bones; great toe has two phalanges | — |

## Result

The bones of the appendicular skeleton were identified, their landmarks were noted, and the side of the long bones was determined.

## Precautions

1. Hold bones in the anatomical position before deciding the side.
2. Handle bones carefully over the table.
3. Do not write on the bones.

## Viva questions

1. **How many bones are in each upper limb?** 30 (60 in both).
2. **Name the three bones that form the hip bone.** Ilium, ischium and pubis.
3. **Which is the longest bone of the body?** Femur.
4. **Which bone forms the point of the elbow?** Olecranon process of the ulna.
5. **Which is the largest tarsal bone?** Calcaneus.
6. **Which is the commonly fractured bone of the shoulder girdle?** Clavicle.
7. **What is the acetabulum?** The socket on the hip bone that receives the head of the femur.

# Introduction to haemocytometry

**Aim:** To study the parts of the haemocytometer (improved Neubauer counting chamber and diluting pipettes) and the calculations used for blood cell counts.

> Wear gloves; treat all blood as potentially infectious and discard lancets in a sharps container.

## Principle

Blood has too many cells to count directly. A known volume of blood is **diluted** by a known amount with a fluid that preserves (or removes) particular cells, and the cells in a **known volume** of the diluted blood are counted in a chamber of fixed depth and ruled area. The count per mm³ of undiluted blood is then calculated:

**Cells per mm³ = (cells counted × dilution factor) ÷ volume counted (mm³)**

## Requirements

Haemocytometer set: improved Neubauer chamber with special thick cover slip, RBC pipette, WBC pipette, rubber suction tube; compound microscope; sterile lancet, spirit swabs, cotton.

## The counting chamber

```text
Improved Neubauer ruling (total 3 mm x 3 mm = 9 large squares of 1 mm2)
 _________________________________
|  W      |               |    W  |   W = corner squares (each 1 mm2,
| (16 sq) |   CENTRAL     | (16 sq)|       divided into 16) - WBC count
|_________|   SQUARE      |_______|
|         | 25 medium sq. |       |   Central square (1 mm2) has
|         | each with 16  |       |   25 medium squares (each 0.04 mm2)
|_________| small squares |_______|   x 16 = 400 smallest squares
|  W      | (R = 4 corner |    W  |   (each 1/400 mm2 = 0.0025 mm2)
|         |  + 1 centre   |       |
|_________|  medium sq.)__|_______|   R = squares used for RBC count
 Depth between chamber floor and cover slip = 0.1 mm
```

| Area | Size | Volume (× 0.1 mm depth) | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One large square | 1 mm² | 0.1 mm³ | WBC (4 corner squares = 0.4 mm³) |
| One medium square (central area) | 1/25 mm² = 0.04 mm² | 0.004 mm³ | RBC (5 squares = 0.02 mm³) |
| One smallest square | 1/400 mm² | 1/4000 mm³ = 0.00025 mm³ | 80 smallest squares in 5 medium squares |

## Diluting pipettes

| Feature | RBC pipette | WBC pipette |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bead in bulb | Red | White |
| Marks | 0.5, 1, 101 | 0.5, 1, 11 |
| Volume of bulb | 100 parts | 10 parts |
| Blood drawn to | 0.5 | 0.5 |
| Diluting fluid to | 101 | 11 |
| Dilution | 0.5 in 100 = **1 in 200** | 0.5 in 10 = **1 in 20** |
| Diluting fluid | Hayem's fluid | Turk's fluid |

The fluid in the stem (below the bulb) does not mix and is discarded before charging the chamber, which is why only the bulb volume counts in the dilution.

## Procedure (general)

1. Clean and dry the chamber, cover slip and pipettes. Place the cover slip over the ruled area.
2. Clean the fingertip with spirit, let it dry, prick with a sterile lancet, wipe the first drop, and use the next free-flowing drop.
3. Suck blood exactly to the 0.5 mark; wipe the tip; then suck diluting fluid to the 101 (RBC) or 11 (WBC) mark.
4. Hold the pipette horizontally, close both ends and shake for 2–3 minutes to mix.
5. Discard the first few drops (stem fluid). Touch the tip to the edge of the cover slip so the fluid fills the chamber by capillary action without overflow or bubbles.
6. Allow cells to settle for 2–3 minutes, then count under the microscope (low power for WBCs, high power for RBCs).
7. **Counting rule:** count cells lying inside a square and those touching the **upper and left** borders; ignore those touching the lower and right borders, so no cell is counted twice.

## Calculations

**WBC count:** cells in 4 large corner squares = N.
WBC per mm³ = N × 20 ÷ 0.4 = **N × 50**.

**RBC count:** cells in 5 medium squares (80 smallest squares) = N.
RBC per mm³ = N × 200 ÷ 0.02 = **N × 10,000**.

## Result

The parts of the haemocytometer, the dilution factors (RBC 1:200, WBC 1:20) and the formulae for RBC (N × 10,000) and WBC (N × 50) counts were studied.

## Precautions

1. Use separate, clean, dry pipettes; never mix up RBC and WBC pipettes.
2. Fill exactly to the marks; air bubbles in the pipette make the result wrong.
3. Do not overfill the chamber; fluid must not run into the moats.
4. Clean pipettes after use with water, alcohol and ether (or as directed) so blood does not clot inside.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the depth of the Neubauer chamber?** 0.1 mm.
2. **What is the area of the smallest square?** 1/400 mm².
3. **Why does the RBC pipette have a red bead?** For identification, and the bead helps mix blood with the fluid.
4. **What is the dilution in the WBC pipette?** 1 in 20.
5. **Why are the first drops discarded?** They contain only diluting fluid from the stem.
6. **Why does the cover slip have to be special?** It is thick and optically flat so the depth stays exactly 0.1 mm.
practicals.title: Introduction to haemocytometry

# Total white blood cell (WBC) count

**Aim:** To determine the total number of white blood cells per mm³ of blood using the haemocytometer.

> Wear gloves; use a fresh sterile lancet; dispose of sharps safely.

## Principle

Blood is diluted 1 in 20 with **Turk's fluid**, which lyses red cells and stains white cell nuclei so that the leucocytes can be counted. WBCs in the four large corner squares (total volume 0.4 mm³) of the Neubauer chamber are counted and the number per mm³ of blood is calculated.

**Turk's fluid:** dilute glacial acetic acid (about 1.5 ml per 100 ml; lyses RBCs) with a little 1% gentian violet (about 1 ml per 100 ml; stains WBC nuclei) in distilled water.

## Requirements

Neubauer chamber with cover slip, WBC pipette (white bead, marks 0.5 and 11), Turk's fluid, microscope, sterile lancet, spirit swabs, cotton.

## Procedure

1. Clean the chamber and cover slip; place the cover slip in position.
2. Prick the cleaned fingertip; wipe off the first drop.
3. Draw blood into the WBC pipette exactly to the **0.5** mark; wipe the outside of the tip.
4. Draw Turk's fluid to the **11** mark (dilution 1 in 20).
5. Mix by rolling the pipette horizontally for 2–3 minutes.
6. Discard the first 2–3 drops; charge the chamber by touching the tip to the edge of the cover slip.
7. Wait 2–3 minutes for cells to settle.
8. Under low power (10×), count WBCs (dark-stained dots with visible nuclei) in the **four corner large squares**, following the upper-and-left border rule.

## Observations and calculation

| Square | Cells counted |
| --- | --- |
| Upper left | n1 |
| Upper right | n2 |
| Lower left | n3 |
| Lower right | n4 |
| Total (N) | n1 + n2 + n3 + n4 |

Volume counted = 4 squares × 1 mm² × 0.1 mm = 0.4 mm³.

**WBC per mm³ = N × dilution ÷ volume = N × 20 ÷ 0.4 = N × 50**

**Worked example:** cells counted = 38 + 42 + 35 + 40 = 155. WBC = 155 × 50 = **7,750 per mm³** (within normal range).

**Normal range:** 4,000–11,000 per mm³ in adults (higher in newborns). Above 11,000 = leucocytosis (bacterial infection, leukaemia); below 4,000 = leucopenia (typhoid, some viral infections, marrow suppression).

## Result

The total WBC count of the given blood sample is ______ per mm³.

## Precautions

1. Fill the pipette exactly to the marks without air bubbles.
2. Mix thoroughly so cells are evenly spread.
3. Do not overfill the chamber.
4. Count carefully using the border rule; count each square only once.
5. Clean the pipette immediately after use.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the function of acetic acid in Turk's fluid?** It lyses (destroys) red cells so they do not hide the WBCs.
2. **Why is gentian violet added?** It stains the nuclei of WBCs, making them easy to see.
3. **What is the dilution factor?** 20.
4. **What is the multiplication factor?** 50.
5. **What is leucocytosis?** A total WBC count above about 11,000 per mm³, as in acute bacterial infection.
6. **Why are nucleated RBCs (in some diseases) counted as WBCs?** They are not lysed and their nuclei stain; a correction is applied using the differential count.
practicals.title: Total white blood cell (WBC) count

practicals.markdown:
# Total red blood cell (RBC) count

**Aim:** To determine the total number of red blood cells per mm³ of blood using the haemocytometer.

> Wear gloves; use a fresh sterile lancet; dispose of sharps safely.

## Principle

Blood is diluted 1 in 200 with **Hayem's fluid**, an isotonic fluid that keeps red cells intact and separate. RBCs in five medium squares (80 smallest squares; volume 0.02 mm³) of the central large square of the Neubauer chamber are counted and the number per mm³ is calculated.

**Hayem's fluid (per 100 ml distilled water):** sodium chloride 0.5 g (keeps the fluid isotonic), sodium sulphate 2.5 g (prevents clumping and rouleaux), mercuric chloride 0.25 g (preservative, prevents fungal growth).

## Requirements

Neubauer chamber with cover slip, RBC pipette (red bead, marks 0.5 and 101), Hayem's fluid, microscope, sterile lancet, spirit swabs, cotton.

## Procedure

1. Clean the chamber and fix the cover slip.
2. Prick the cleaned fingertip; wipe off the first drop.
3. Draw blood exactly to the **0.5** mark of the RBC pipette; wipe the tip.
4. Draw Hayem's fluid to the **101** mark (dilution 1 in 200).
5. Mix by rotating the pipette horizontally for 2–3 minutes.
6. Discard the first few drops and charge the chamber.
7. Wait 2–3 minutes for the cells to settle.
8. Under high power (40×), count RBCs in **five medium squares** of the central square — the four corner ones and the centre one — each having 16 smallest squares. Use the upper-and-left border rule.

## Observations and calculation

| Medium square | Cells counted |
| --- | --- |
| Upper left | n1 |
| Upper right | n2 |
| Centre | n3 |
| Lower left | n4 |
| Lower right | n5 |
| Total (N) | n1 + … + n5 |

Volume counted = 80 smallest squares × (1/400 mm²) × 0.1 mm = 0.02 mm³.

**RBC per mm³ = N × 200 ÷ 0.02 = N × 10,000**

**Worked example:** cells counted = 98 + 102 + 95 + 100 + 105 = 500. RBC = 500 × 10,000 = **5,000,000 (5.0 million) per mm³**.

**Normal range:** about 4.5–5.5 million/mm³ in adult men and 4.0–5.0 million/mm³ in women. A low count suggests anaemia; a high count, polycythaemia (high altitude, chronic lung disease).

## Result

The total RBC count of the given blood sample is ______ million per mm³.

## Precautions

1. Use a clean, dry RBC pipette and fill exactly to the marks.
2. Mix well; uneven mixing gives a falsely high or low count.
3. Charge the chamber in one smooth movement without bubbles or overflow.
4. Count under high power, using the border rule.
5. Clean the pipette immediately after use.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is the dilution higher for RBC than for WBC?** RBCs are about a thousand times more numerous, so they must be diluted more to be countable.
2. **Why must the diluting fluid be isotonic?** So the red cells neither swell and burst nor shrink.
3. **What is the multiplication factor for the RBC count?** 10,000.
4. **Name a physiological cause of a raised RBC count.** Living at high altitude (low oxygen stimulates erythropoietin).
5. **What is the life span of an RBC?** About 120 days.
practicals.title: Total red blood cell (RBC) count

# Determination of bleeding time

**Aim:** To determine the bleeding time of the given subject by Duke's filter paper method.

> Wear gloves; use a fresh sterile lancet for every subject; dispose of sharps safely.

## Principle

**Bleeding time** is the time from a standard skin puncture until bleeding stops on its own. It depends mainly on **platelet function** and **constriction of small vessels** (vascular spasm and platelet plug), not on clotting factors. In Duke's method, blood from a puncture is blotted on filter paper every 30 seconds until no more stain appears.

## Requirements

Sterile disposable lancet, spirit swabs, dry cotton, circular filter paper, stopwatch.

## Procedure

1. Clean the fingertip (or ear lobe) with spirit and let it dry completely.
2. Make a puncture about 3 mm deep with a sterile lancet, without squeezing. **Start the stopwatch** as blood appears.
3. Every **30 seconds**, gently touch the filter paper to the drop of blood without touching the skin, using a fresh area of the paper each time.
4. Continue until the paper no longer picks up any blood. **Stop the watch.**
5. Count the blood spots on the paper.

## Observations and calculation

Each spot represents 30 seconds.

**Bleeding time = number of spots × 30 seconds**

| Observation | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Number of blood spots | n |
| Bleeding time | n × 30 s |

**Worked example:** 5 spots → 5 × 30 = 150 s = **2 minutes 30 seconds**. The spots become smaller in size one after the other.

**Normal value:** about 1–5 minutes (Duke's method).

**Prolonged in:** thrombocytopenia (low platelets, e.g. purpura), platelet function defects, aspirin use, von Willebrand disease, scurvy (fragile vessels). It is usually **normal in haemophilia**, because platelets and vessels are normal.

## Result

The bleeding time of the given subject is ______ minutes.

## Precautions

1. Let the spirit dry before puncturing; spirit delays clotting and spreads blood.
2. Do not squeeze the finger.
3. Do not touch the wound with the filter paper; this disturbs the platelet plug.
4. Use a fresh part of the filter paper every 30 seconds.

## Viva questions

1. **What does bleeding time mainly test?** Platelet function and vascular response.
2. **Is bleeding time prolonged in haemophilia?** Usually no; clotting time is prolonged instead.
3. **Name a drug that prolongs bleeding time.** Aspirin (it reduces platelet thromboxane A2).
4. **What is the normal bleeding time?** About 1–5 minutes.
5. **Why should the finger not be squeezed?** Squeezing forces tissue fluid out and gives a wrong result.
practicals.title: Determination of bleeding time

practicals.markdown:
# Determination of clotting time

**Aim:** To determine the clotting time of the given subject's blood by the capillary tube method.

> Wear gloves; use a fresh sterile lancet; dispose of sharps and broken glass safely.

## Principle

**Clotting time (coagulation time)** is the time from the moment blood leaves the vessel until it forms a fibrin clot. It reflects the **clotting factors** of the intrinsic and common pathways. Blood is drawn into a fine glass capillary; pieces of the tube are broken off at intervals until fibrin threads are seen between the broken ends.

## Requirements

Plain glass capillary tubes (about 10 cm long, 1 mm bore), sterile lancet, spirit swabs, cotton, stopwatch.

## Procedure

1. Clean the fingertip with spirit and allow it to dry.
2. Make a fairly deep prick so that blood flows freely. **Start the stopwatch** when blood first appears.
3. Hold one end of the capillary tube to the drop and let blood fill most of the tube by capillary action (keep the other end slightly lower).
4. After about 2 minutes, break off a small piece (about 1 cm) from one end every **30 seconds**, separating the pieces slowly.
5. When a thin **fibrin thread** is seen stretching between the broken pieces, **stop the watch**.

## Observations and calculation

| Observation | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Time when blood appeared | 0 s |
| Time when fibrin thread first seen | t |
| Clotting time | t |

**Worked example:** breaks at 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0 minutes; fibrin thread first seen at 4.0 minutes → clotting time = **4 minutes**.

**Normal value:** about 3–8 minutes by the capillary tube method (normal ranges differ with the method).

**Prolonged in:** haemophilia (factor VIII or IX deficiency), vitamin K deficiency, obstructive jaundice, severe liver disease, anticoagulant therapy (heparin). Clotting time is a rough screening test; laboratories use more precise tests such as prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time.

## Result

The clotting time of the given subject's blood is ______ minutes.

## Precautions

1. Allow the spirit to dry before pricking.
2. Blood must flow freely; do not squeeze the finger.
3. Use a clean, dry capillary of uniform bore.
4. Break the tube gently and pull the pieces apart slowly so a thin thread is not missed.
5. Keep the room temperature normal; cold delays clotting.

## Viva questions

1. **Difference between bleeding time and clotting time?** Bleeding time tests platelets and vessels; clotting time tests clotting factors.
2. **In which disease is clotting time prolonged but bleeding time normal?** Haemophilia.
3. **Which vitamin is needed for the synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X?** Vitamin K.
4. **What is the normal clotting time by the capillary method?** About 3–8 minutes.
5. **Name an anticoagulant used in blood banks.** Sodium citrate (citrate-based solutions).
practicals.title: Determination of clotting time

# Estimation of haemoglobin (Sahli's method)

**Aim:** To estimate the haemoglobin content of the given blood sample by Sahli's acid haematin method.

> Wear gloves; handle hydrochloric acid with care; use a fresh sterile lancet.

## Principle

Haemoglobin is converted to brown **acid haematin** by N/10 (0.1 N) hydrochloric acid. The brown solution is diluted with distilled water until its colour matches the standard brown glass rods of the comparator. The haemoglobin concentration in g/dL (g%) is read directly from the graduated tube.

## Requirements

Sahli's haemoglobinometer (comparator with standard brown glass rods, graduated haemoglobin tube marked in g/dL, haemoglobin pipette marked at 20 mm³ = 0.02 ml, glass stirrer), N/10 HCl, distilled water, dropper, sterile lancet, spirit swabs.

```text
   [comparator box]
   | brown  |  graduated   |  brown |
   | glass  |  tube (g/dL) |  glass |
   | rod    |  acid        |  rod   |
   |        |  haematin    |        |
   |________|______________|________|
     white opal glass background behind
```

## Procedure

1. Fill the graduated tube with N/10 HCl up to the lowest mark (mark 2 g/dL, or 10% on the percentage scale).
2. Clean and prick the fingertip; wipe the first drop.
3. Suck blood into the haemoglobin pipette exactly to the **20 mm³** mark; wipe the outside of the tip.
4. Blow the blood into the bottom of the acid in the tube; rinse the pipette two or three times with the acid in the tube so no blood remains.
5. Mix with the stirrer and allow to stand for **10 minutes** for full conversion to acid haematin.
6. Add distilled water drop by drop, stirring after each addition, and compare the colour with the standard rods against the light.
7. Stop when the colour exactly matches. Read the lower meniscus in g/dL. Add one more drop and read again; take the reading where the match is best.

## Observations

| Reading | Value (g/dL) |
| --- | --- |
| First match | |
| After one more drop | |
| Haemoglobin (best match) | |

**Worked example:** colour matches at 14.2 g/dL and is slightly lighter at 14.4 g/dL → haemoglobin = **14.2 g/dL**.

**Normal values:** about 14–18 g/dL in adult men, 12–16 g/dL in adult women; higher in newborns. Low values suggest anaemia; high values, polycythaemia or dehydration.

**Useful calculation:** O2-carrying capacity ≈ Hb (g/dL) × 1.34 ml O2/g. For Hb 15 g/dL → about 20 ml O2 per 100 ml of blood.

## Result

The haemoglobin content of the given blood sample is ______ g/dL.

## Precautions

1. Draw blood exactly to the 20 mm³ mark without air bubbles.
2. Wait the full 10 minutes before diluting; conversion to acid haematin is slow.
3. Add water drop by drop; once over-diluted, the test must be repeated.
4. Compare colours in daylight against the white background.
5. Rinse the pipette with acid so all blood enters the tube.

## Viva questions

1. **What compound is formed in Sahli's method?** Acid haematin (brown).
2. **Why wait for 10 minutes?** For complete conversion of haemoglobin to acid haematin.
3. **What is a source of error?** Subjective colour matching; acid haematin colour also develops slowly.
4. **Normal Hb in adult women?** About 12–16 g/dL.
5. **How much oxygen can 1 g of Hb carry?** About 1.34 ml.
practicals.title: Estimation of haemoglobin (Sahli's method)

practicals.markdown:
# Determination of blood group

**Aim:** To determine the ABO blood group and Rh type of the given blood sample by the slide method.

> Wear gloves; use a fresh sterile lancet; discard slides and lancets safely.

## Principle

Red cells carry antigens A, B and D (Rh). When blood is mixed with a serum containing the matching antibody, the red cells clump (**agglutination**), visible as fine or coarse granules. Agglutination with anti-A means antigen A is present, with anti-B antigen B, and with anti-D the cells are Rh positive.

## Requirements

Anti-A (blue), anti-B (yellow) and anti-D antisera, clean glass slide or white tile marked A, B and D, sterile lancet, spirit swabs, separate toothpicks or applicator sticks, (normal saline if the blood is to be diluted).

## Procedure

1. Mark a clean slide with three areas: A, B and D.
2. Place one drop of anti-A, anti-B and anti-D in the respective areas.
3. Clean and prick the fingertip; put one small drop of blood next to each antiserum drop.
4. Mix each pair with a **separate** stick, spreading over a small area.
5. Rock the slide gently for about 2 minutes and look for clumping against a white background (anti-D may need slightly longer; read within the time stated by the kit maker).

## Observations

| Anti-A | Anti-B | Anti-D | Blood group |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| + | − | + | A positive |
| − | + | + | B positive |
| + | + | + | AB positive |
| − | − | + | O positive |
| + | − | − | A negative |
| − | + | − | B negative |
| + | + | − | AB negative |
| − | − | − | O negative |

(+ = agglutination; − = no agglutination, uniform red mixture)

```text
   A            B            D
 [ :.:: ]    [ ~~~~ ]    [ :.:: ]     example result:
 clumps      smooth      clumps       A positive
```

## Result

The blood group of the given subject is ______ (ABO) and Rh ______.

## Precautions

1. Use a separate stick for each antiserum to avoid carrying antibodies across.
2. Do not use too much blood; a large excess of cells can hide weak agglutination.
3. Do not let the mixture dry; drying can look like clumping.
4. Check that antisera are within expiry and stored cold as directed.
5. Read the result within the stated time.

## Viva questions

1. **What is agglutination?** Clumping of red cells when their antigen meets the matching antibody.
2. **Which group is the universal donor and why?** O negative (red cells), because the cells carry no A, B or D antigens.
3. **Which group is the universal recipient?** AB positive, because the plasma has no anti-A or anti-B.
4. **What is the Rh factor?** The D antigen on red cells.
5. **Why is blood grouping important?** For safe transfusion, organ transplantation, and preventing Rh disease of the newborn; also used in paternity and forensic work.
6. **Is anti-D naturally present in Rh-negative people?** No; it forms only after exposure to Rh-positive cells.

# Determination of erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)

**Aim:** To determine the erythrocyte sedimentation rate of the given blood sample by the Westergren method.

> Venous blood is collected by a trained person. Wear gloves and handle blood safely.

## Principle

When anticoagulated blood stands in a vertical tube, red cells settle because they are heavier than plasma. The **distance (mm) the top of the red cell column falls in one hour** is the ESR. Settling is faster when red cells stack into **rouleaux**, which happens when plasma fibrinogen and globulins rise (inflammation, infection, pregnancy). ESR is not specific for any disease but shows that inflammation or tissue damage is present and helps follow its course.

## Requirements

Westergren tube (200 mm graduated, 2.5 mm bore) and stand, 3.8% sodium citrate solution, syringe and needle (or vacuum tube), small test tube, timer.

## Procedure

1. Take 0.4 ml of 3.8% sodium citrate in a test tube and add 1.6 ml of venous blood (ratio 1 part citrate : 4 parts blood); mix gently by inversion.
2. Draw the mixed blood into the Westergren tube exactly to the **0 mark** without bubbles.
3. Fix the tube **exactly vertical** in the stand, away from vibration, heat and sunlight. Start the timer.
4. After exactly **one hour**, read the height of the clear plasma column above the red cells in millimetres.

## Observations

| Time | Reading |
| --- | --- |
| Start | 0 mm |
| After 1 hour | ____ mm |

**Worked example:** the top of the red cell column has fallen to the 12 mark after one hour → ESR = **12 mm in the first hour** (normal for an adult man).

**Normal values (Westergren):** about 0–15 mm in 1 hour for men and 0–20 mm for women; slightly higher in older people.

| ESR raised | ESR lowered |
| --- | --- |
| Pregnancy, menstruation, anaemia, tuberculosis, rheumatoid arthritis, rheumatic fever, acute infections, multiple myeloma, some cancers | Polycythaemia, sickle cell disease, high plasma albumin, very low fibrinogen |

## Result

The ESR of the given blood sample is ______ mm in the first hour (Westergren).

## Precautions

1. Use the correct citrate-to-blood ratio (1 : 4).
2. Keep the tube exactly vertical; even a slight tilt speeds sedimentation.
3. Avoid bubbles, vibration and direct heat.
4. Do the test within a few hours of collection.
5. Read exactly at one hour.

## Viva questions

1. **What is rouleaux formation?** Stacking of red cells like a pile of coins, which makes them settle faster.
2. **Which plasma proteins raise the ESR?** Fibrinogen and globulins.
3. **Name the anticoagulant used in the Westergren method.** 3.8% sodium citrate.
4. **Is ESR specific for one disease?** No; it is a non-specific marker of inflammation.
5. **Name a condition with low ESR.** Polycythaemia.
6. **What other method is used?** The Wintrobe method (100 mm tube).

# Determination of heart rate and pulse rate

**Aim:** To determine the heart rate by auscultation and the pulse rate by palpation of the radial artery, and to examine the radial pulse.

## Principle

Each ventricular contraction produces the heart sounds (heard at the apex with a stethoscope) and sends a pressure wave along the arteries, felt as the **pulse**. In a healthy person heart rate and pulse rate are equal. If some beats are too weak to reach the wrist (for example in atrial fibrillation), the pulse rate is lower than the heart rate; the difference is the **pulse deficit**.

## Requirements

Stethoscope, watch with a second hand (or stopwatch), couch.

## Procedure

**A. Pulse rate**

1. Let the subject sit or lie quietly for 5 minutes.
2. Place the tips of your index, middle and ring fingers on the radial artery at the front of the wrist, just lateral to the flexor tendons (thumb side). Do not use your thumb, which has its own pulse.
3. Press gently until the pulse is felt. Count the beats for a **full minute**.
4. Note the rhythm (regular/irregular), volume (strength) and condition of the vessel wall; compare both wrists.

**B. Heart rate**

1. Place the diaphragm of the stethoscope over the **apex beat** — left fifth intercostal space, just medial to the midclavicular line.
2. Count the heart sounds (one "lub-dub" = one beat) for one full minute.
3. If the rhythm is irregular, count heart rate and pulse rate at the same time (two observers) to find any pulse deficit.

**C. Effect of exercise (optional)**

1. Ask the subject to do mild exercise (e.g. 20 squats) and count the pulse again immediately and every minute until it returns to the resting value.

## Observations

| Condition | Pulse rate (per min) | Heart rate (per min) | Rhythm | Volume |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rest (sitting) | | | | |
| After exercise | | | | |
| Recovery (minutes taken) | | | | |

**Worked example:** pulse at rest 72/min, heart rate 72/min, regular, good volume; after exercise 110/min; back to 74/min after 3 minutes. Pulse deficit = 72 − 72 = 0.

**Normal values:** 60–100 per minute in adults (average about 72); higher in children and infants. Above 100 = tachycardia; below 60 = bradycardia (normal in trained athletes and during sleep).

**Factors increasing the rate:** exercise, emotion, fever, anaemia, pregnancy, hyperthyroidism, adrenaline. **Decreasing:** sleep, athletic training, raised intracranial pressure, hypothyroidism, β-blockers.

## Result

1. The resting pulse rate of the subject is ______ per minute, regular, of normal volume.
2. The heart rate of the subject is ______ per minute; pulse deficit ______.

## Precautions

1. Subject should be relaxed; count after rest.
2. Count for a full minute, especially if the rhythm is irregular.
3. Do not palpate with the thumb.
4. Do not press too hard; you may stop the pulse.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the pulse?** The rhythmic expansion of an artery wall caused by the pressure wave of ventricular ejection.
2. **Where is the apex beat felt?** Left fifth intercostal space, just medial to the midclavicular line.
3. **What is pulse deficit?** Heart rate minus pulse rate; seen in atrial fibrillation.
4. **Name other sites for feeling the pulse.** Carotid, brachial, femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, temporal.
5. **What is sinus arrhythmia?** Normal increase in heart rate during inspiration and decrease in expiration, common in young people.
6. **Why is the heart rate low in athletes?** Higher vagal tone and larger stroke volume.

# Recording of blood pressure

**Aim:** To record the arterial blood pressure of the given subject by the palpatory and auscultatory methods using a sphygmomanometer.

## Principle

A cuff wrapped around the arm is inflated until it compresses the brachial artery completely. As the pressure in the cuff is slowly released, blood begins to spurt through the partly opened artery when cuff pressure falls just below **systolic pressure**, producing tapping sounds (**Korotkoff sounds**) heard with a stethoscope below the cuff. The sounds disappear when cuff pressure falls below **diastolic pressure** and flow becomes smooth again.

**Korotkoff phases:** I — first clear tapping (systolic pressure); II — murmuring; III — louder, crisper sounds; IV — sudden muffling; V — disappearance (diastolic pressure in adults).

## Requirements

Sphygmomanometer (mercury, aneroid or digital with a cuff of suitable size), stethoscope, couch or chair.

## Procedure

1. Let the subject rest for at least 5 minutes, seated with the arm supported at heart level, palm up. No smoking, coffee or exercise in the previous 30 minutes.
2. Wrap the deflated cuff evenly around the bare upper arm, its lower edge about 2–3 cm above the elbow crease, with the centre of the bladder over the brachial artery.
3. **Palpatory method:** feel the radial pulse; close the valve and inflate until the pulse disappears; inflate about 30 mmHg more; deflate slowly (2–3 mmHg per second) and note the reading when the pulse reappears — the palpatory systolic pressure.
4. Deflate completely and wait about a minute.
5. **Auscultatory method:** place the stethoscope diaphragm over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa (medial to the biceps tendon), not under the cuff. Inflate to about 30 mmHg above the palpatory systolic value.
6. Deflate at 2–3 mmHg per second. Note the pressure at the **first tapping sound** (systolic) and when the sounds **disappear** (diastolic).
7. Deflate fully, remove the cuff, repeat after 1–2 minutes and record the average. Optionally record lying, standing and after exercise.

## Observations and calculation

| Position / condition | Systolic (mmHg) | Diastolic (mmHg) | Pulse pressure | Mean arterial pressure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sitting (palpatory) | | — | — | — |
| Sitting (auscultatory) | | | | |
| Standing | | | | |
| After exercise | | | | |

**Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic.** **Mean arterial pressure (MAP) = diastolic + (pulse pressure ÷ 3).**

**Worked example:** BP = 120/80 mmHg → pulse pressure = 40 mmHg; MAP = 80 + 40/3 ≈ **93 mmHg**.

**Normal adult value:** about 120/80 mmHg. A persistent reading at or above about 140/90 mmHg suggests hypertension (it must be confirmed on repeated readings); low readings with symptoms suggest hypotension.

## Result

The blood pressure of the subject in the sitting position is ______ / ______ mmHg (auscultatory method); pulse pressure ______ mmHg; MAP ______ mmHg.

## Precautions

1. Use a cuff of the correct size; a narrow cuff gives falsely high values.
2. Keep the arm and the manometer at heart level; read mercury at eye level.
3. Do not inflate unnecessarily high or keep the cuff inflated for long.
4. Deflate at a steady 2–3 mmHg per second.
5. Always do the palpatory method first to avoid missing the auscultatory gap.

## Viva questions

1. **What are Korotkoff sounds?** Sounds produced by turbulent flow through a partly compressed artery as cuff pressure is released.
2. **Why is the palpatory method done first?** To find the approximate systolic pressure and avoid errors from the auscultatory gap (a silent interval in some people).
3. **What is pulse pressure?** Systolic minus diastolic pressure (normally about 40 mmHg).
4. **Name the receptors that regulate BP quickly.** Baroreceptors of the carotid sinus and aortic arch.
5. **Why does systolic pressure rise on exercise?** Cardiac output increases.
6. **What happens to BP on standing up suddenly?** It falls slightly, but the baroreceptor reflex quickly restores it.

5. Vitamin B12 and folic acid for DNA synthesis (deficiency → megaloblastic anaemia); intrinsic factor for B12 absorption.
6. Iron, proteins, vitamin C, copper, cobalt, vitamin B6; hormones such as thyroxine and androgens.
7. Hb synthesis: succinyl-CoA + glycine → ALA → porphobilinogen → protoporphyrin IX + Fe2+ → haem; haem + globin chain → subunit; four subunits form Hb.
8. HbA = α2β2, HbF = α2γ2; four haems carry four O2; normal 14–18 g/dL (men), 12–16 g/dL (women).
9. Breakdown: globin → amino acids; iron → ferritin/transferrin; haem → biliverdin → bilirubin → bile.
10. Flow chart of erythropoiesis.
questions.question: Define haemopoiesis. Describe the stages of erythropoiesis and the factors affecting it. Add a note on formation of haemoglobin.

questions.answer:
1. Components: lymph, lymphatic vessels, lymphatic organs and tissues.
2. Lymph: interstitial fluid in lymph vessels; less protein than plasma; chyle from intestine is milky.
3. Lymph capillaries: blind-ended, overlapping endothelial flaps; lacteals absorb fat.
4. Vessels with valves → nodes → trunks → thoracic duct (cisterna chyli; drains lower body and left upper body into left subclavian–internal jugular junction) and right lymphatic duct (right upper body).
5. Lymph flow aided by skeletal muscle pump, breathing, smooth muscle of vessels, valves; about 3 L returned daily.
6. Primary organs: red bone marrow, thymus. Secondary: lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils, MALT, Peyer's patches.
7. Lymph node: capsule, trabeculae, cortex with follicles (B cells), paracortex (T cells), medulla with sinuses; several afferent and one or two efferent vessels at the hilum; diagram.
8. Spleen: white pulp (immune), red pulp (removes old RBCs, platelet store).
9. Functions: return of fluid and proteins, fat absorption, immunity, filtration.
10. Disorders: lymphoedema, filariasis, lymphadenitis, spread of cancer.
questions.question: Describe the lymphatic system: lymphatic organs and tissues, lymph vessels, lymph circulation and functions. Draw a labelled diagram of a lymph node.

questions.answer:
1. Blood volume 5–6 L, pH 7.35–7.45; plasma about 55%, formed elements about 45%.
2. Plasma: water 91–92%, proteins (albumin, globulins, fibrinogen), nutrients, electrolytes, wastes, hormones, gases.
3. Formed elements: RBC 4.5–5.5 million/mm³, WBC 4,000–11,000/mm³, platelets 1.5–4 lakh/mm³.
4. Functions — transport (O2, CO2, nutrients, wastes, hormones, drugs); regulation (temperature, pH buffering, water balance).
5. Protection (immunity by WBCs and antibodies; clotting by platelets and plasma factors).
questions.question: Write the composition and functions of blood.

questions.answer:
1. ABO: antigens A and B on RBCs; plasma has antibodies against the missing antigen; groups A, B, AB, O.
2. O is universal donor (no antigens); AB universal recipient (no antibodies); incompatible transfusion causes agglutination and haemolysis.
3. Rh: D antigen present → Rh positive; anti-D is not natural, forms only after exposure.
4. Erythroblastosis fetalis: Rh-negative mother sensitised by first Rh-positive baby; in the next pregnancy maternal anti-D crosses placenta and destroys fetal RBCs → anaemia, jaundice, oedema.
5. Prevention: anti-D immunoglobulin to the mother within 72 hours after delivery or sensitising events.
questions.question: Explain the ABO blood group system and the Rh factor. What is erythroblastosis fetalis?

questions.answer:
1. Anaemia: reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of blood due to fewer RBCs or less Hb; symptoms — fatigue, pallor, breathlessness, palpitations.
2. Haemorrhagic (blood loss) and iron-deficiency anaemia (microcytic hypochromic; commonest in India).
3. Megaloblastic anaemia from vitamin B12 or folate lack; pernicious anaemia from lack of intrinsic factor (macrocytic).
4. Haemolytic anaemia: sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, G6PD deficiency, mismatched transfusion, malaria; aplastic anaemia (marrow failure).
5. Morphological classes: normocytic normochromic, microcytic hypochromic, macrocytic.

questions.answer:
1. Network of phagocytic cells derived from monocytes (mononuclear phagocyte system).
2. Cells: monocytes (blood), Kupffer cells (liver), alveolar macrophages (lung), microglia (brain), Langerhans cells (skin), histiocytes (connective tissue), macrophages in spleen, lymph nodes and marrow, osteoclasts.
3. Phagocytosis of bacteria, dead cells and debris.
4. Destruction of old RBCs, haemoglobin breakdown to bilirubin, iron storage.
5. Antigen presentation and cytokine release in immunity.
questions.question: Write a note on the reticulo-endothelial system.

questions.answer:
1. Uses: severe haemorrhage, severe anaemia, surgery, burns, clotting disorders, exchange transfusion in newborn; component therapy (packed cells, platelets, plasma).
2. Precautions: ABO and Rh grouping, cross-matching, screening for HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis, malaria; proper storage.
3. Haemolytic reaction from mismatch: fever, chills, back pain, haemoglobinuria, kidney failure, shock.
4. Febrile and allergic reactions; circulatory overload; infection transmission.

1. ANS controls cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands; two-neuron chain with ganglion.
2. Sympathetic: thoracolumbar outflow T1–L2; short preganglionic, long postganglionic fibres; paravertebral chain and prevertebral ganglia (coeliac, superior and inferior mesenteric).
3. Sympathetic transmitters: ACh at ganglia (nicotinic), noradrenaline at effectors (α, β); sweat glands cholinergic; adrenal medulla releases adrenaline.
4. Parasympathetic: craniosacral outflow (CN III, VII, IX, X; S2–S4); long preganglionic, short postganglionic; terminal ganglia near organs; vagus carries most fibres.
5. Parasympathetic transmitter: ACh at both synapses (nicotinic, then muscarinic).
6. Diagram of outflows.
7. Sympathetic effects: pupil dilation, raised heart rate and force, bronchodilation, gut inhibition, glycogenolysis, bladder relaxation, sweating — fight or flight.
8. Parasympathetic effects: miosis, accommodation, slower heart, bronchoconstriction, increased gut motility and secretion, bladder emptying, salivation — rest and digest.
9. Comparison table: origin, ganglion position, fibre lengths, transmitter, distribution, overall effect.
10. Dual innervation and autonomic tone; drugs (atropine, propranolol, salbutamol, pilocarpine).
questions.question: Describe the structure and functions of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems. Compare them in a table.

questions.answer:
1. Eyeball in the orbit with accessory structures: eyelids, conjunctiva, lacrimal apparatus, six extraocular muscles.
2. Fibrous coat: sclera and transparent avascular cornea.
3. Vascular coat (uvea): choroid, ciliary body (ciliary muscle, aqueous humour), iris with pupil (sphincter and dilator pupillae).
4. Nervous coat: retina with rods (dim light, rhodopsin, vitamin A) and cones (colour, fovea); optic disc = blind spot.
5. Lens held by suspensory ligaments; aqueous humour drained by canal of Schlemm; vitreous body; labelled diagram.
6. Vision: refraction by cornea and lens → inverted image on retina.
7. Accommodation: ciliary muscle contracts, lens more convex, pupil constricts, eyes converge; pupillary light reflex.
8. Light splits rhodopsin → receptor potential → bipolar and ganglion cells → optic nerve → chiasma → optic tract → lateral geniculate body → occipital visual cortex.
9. Disorders: myopia (concave lens), hypermetropia (convex), presbyopia, astigmatism (cylindrical), cataract, glaucoma.
10. Conjunctivitis, night blindness (vitamin A deficiency), colour blindness.
questions.question: Describe the structure of the eye with a labelled diagram. Explain the mechanism of vision and list common disorders of the eye.

questions.answer:
1. External ear: auricle, external auditory meatus with ceruminous glands, tympanic membrane.
2. Middle ear: air cavity in temporal bone; malleus, incus, stapes; Eustachian tube equalises pressure; oval and round windows.
3. Inner ear: bony labyrinth with perilymph enclosing membranous labyrinth with endolymph; cochlea, vestibule (utricle, saccule), three semicircular canals.
4. Cochlea: organ of Corti with hair cells on basilar membrane under tectorial membrane; diagram of ear.
5. Hearing: sound waves → eardrum → ossicles amplify → stapes at oval window → perilymph waves → basilar membrane vibrates (high pitch at base) → hair cells bend → cochlear nerve → temporal lobe auditory cortex.
6. Round window releases pressure.
7. Balance: utricle and saccule (otoliths) sense head position and linear acceleration; semicircular canal ampullae sense rotation; vestibular nerve → brainstem and cerebellum.
8. Disorders: otitis media, conductive and sensorineural deafness.
9. Ménière's disease, motion sickness, tinnitus, vertigo.
10. Ototoxic drugs such as aminoglycosides.
questions.question: Describe the structure of the ear with a diagram. Explain the mechanism of hearing and of balance. Name common disorders.

questions.answer:
1. I olfactory (S) smell; II optic (S) vision; III oculomotor (M) eye movements, pupil constriction, accommodation; IV trochlear (M) superior oblique.
2. V trigeminal (B) facial sensation, chewing; VI abducens (M) lateral rectus.
3. VII facial (B) facial expression, taste anterior two-thirds, tears and saliva; VIII vestibulocochlear (S) hearing and balance.
4. IX glossopharyngeal (B) taste posterior one-third, swallowing, parotid; X vagus (B) parasympathetic to heart, lungs, gut, voice.
5. XI accessory (M) sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; XII hypoglossal (M) tongue; origins: I cerebrum, II diencephalon, III–IV midbrain, V–VII pons, VIII pons–medulla, IX–XII medulla.
questions.question: Tabulate the cranial nerves with their type and functions.

questions.answer:
1. 31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal.
2. Dorsal root (sensory, dorsal root ganglion) and ventral root (motor) join to form a mixed nerve; branches — dorsal ramus, ventral ramus, meningeal branch, rami communicantes.
3. Cervical plexus C1–C4: phrenic nerve (C3–C5) to diaphragm.
4. Brachial plexus C5–T1: axillary, musculocutaneous, radial, median, ulnar nerves; lumbar plexus L1–L4: femoral, obturator.
5. Sacral plexus L4–S4: sciatic nerve (largest); thoracic nerves T2–T12 form intercostal nerves without a plexus.
questions.question: Describe the origin of spinal nerves and the plexuses they form.

questions.answer:
1. Muscular organ covered by mucous membrane with papillae: filiform (no taste buds), fungiform, circumvallate (most taste buds), foliate.
2. Taste bud: gustatory receptor cells with microvilli at the taste pore, supporting and basal cells; chemicals must dissolve in saliva.
3. Five tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, umami; all regions can detect all tastes.
4. Nerves: facial (anterior two-thirds), glossopharyngeal (posterior one-third), vagus (epiglottis) → medulla → thalamus → gustatory cortex.
5. Disorders: ageusia, hypogeusia, glossitis.
questions.question: Describe the structure of the tongue and the mechanism of taste.

questions.answer:
1. Olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity: olfactory receptor cells (bipolar neurons with cilia), supporting cells, basal stem cells, olfactory glands.
2. Odour molecules dissolve in mucus and bind receptors → nerve impulses.
3. Axons pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid as the olfactory nerve → olfactory bulb → olfactory tract.
4. Cortex in the temporal lobe and limbic system (link to memory and emotion); fast adaptation.
5. Disorders: anosmia, rhinitis, sinusitis.
questions.question: Describe the sense of smell (olfaction) and its pathway.

questions.answer:
1. Myopia: image in front of retina; concave lens. Hypermetropia: image behind retina; convex lens.
2. Presbyopia: age-related loss of lens elasticity; astigmatism: uneven corneal curvature, cylindrical lens.
3. Cataract: lens opacity; surgery with lens replacement.
4. Glaucoma: raised intraocular pressure from poor aqueous drainage → optic nerve damage; drugs such as timolol, pilocarpine.
5. Conjunctivitis, night blindness (vitamin A deficiency), colour blindness (inherited, mostly males).

questions.answer: Malleus, incus and stapes (the stapes is the smallest bone in the body).
questions.question: Name the auditory ossicles.

questions.answer: The optic disc, where the optic nerve leaves the eye; it has no rods or cones, so light falling on it is not seen.
questions.question: What is the blind spot?

1. Location: mediastinum, two-thirds left of midline, apex at left fifth intercostal space; size of a fist, about 250–350 g.
2. Pericardium: fibrous and serous (parietal, visceral) with pericardial fluid.
3. Wall: epicardium, myocardium (thickest in left ventricle), endocardium.
4. Chambers: right and left atria, right and left ventricles; septa (fossa ovalis).
5. Valves: tricuspid, mitral, pulmonary and aortic semilunar; chordae tendineae and papillary muscles.
6. Great vessels: venae cavae, pulmonary trunk, pulmonary veins, aorta.
7. Coronary arteries from aortic sinuses; coronary sinus into right atrium.
8. Labelled diagram.
